newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Congress rolls up sleeves for reform push.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Congress rolls up sleeves for reform push.

text.p: Brazil's Congress begins a new, year-long session later on Monday with the government hoping it can finally get on with approving crucial structural reforms.

Fresh from last week's Carnival break, politicians sounded upbeat about the government's chances of making quick headway with its stop-start reforms of the civil service and the pensions system which have seen little progress since mid-1996.

"I have a feeling, and it is perfectly possible, that the Chamber of Deputies will approve all (the reforms) within the first half of the year," deputy Ubiritan Aguiar, the first secretary of the lower house, told national CBN radio.

Others were more cautious. "The time is right for reform and a June target is within the government's reach. But everything will depend on whether it can work on more than one reform at a time," said Marcelo Cordeiro of consultants Santa Fe Ideias.

Top of the agenda is a second vote in the chamber on a constitutional amendment allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, along with state governors and mayors, to stand for a second, consecutive term.

An aide to deputy Benito Gama, the government's chief whip in the lower house, said leaders of government-allied parties were due to meet Monday or Tuesday to set the second re-election vote for either the last week of February or the first in March.
The amendment, which was given a first approval in the Chamber of Deputies in January, requires a second, three-fifths majority before moving on to the Senate.

Once re-election moves to the upper house, the government wants to put its civil service reform bill to a first Chamber of Deputies vote. The amendment would allow state and municipal governments to dismiss currently unsackable staff and is considered crucial to attempts to reduce public spending.
But it faces stiff opposition within Congress, mainly from lawmakers who would lose out from a $10,400 ceiling on monthly pay and benefits for civil servants included in the bill.
The government is reportedly mulling exempting congressmen from the ceiling in an attempt to smooth passage of the reform.

Another priority for the government is a rewrite in the Senate of its pension reform bill which was stripped of its most important points, including a minimum retirement age for civil service workers, during voting in the lower house last year.
The amendment needs to be approved twice by three-fifths majorities in the upper house before returning to the Chamber of Deputies for another two votes on its new-look text.
Some observers say the government might find it hard to focus the Senate's attention on pension reform at a time when the re-election amendment is also likely to be on its agenda.
"If (new Senate president) Antonio Carlos Magalahes insists on beginning pension reform right now, then it might be back in the lower house before June," said political analyst Cordeiro.

Congress may also be sidetracked from reforms by the government's attempts to renew its Emergency Fiscal Fund, allowing it to sidestep strict constitutional rules on spending and keep its anti-inflation program on track.
The fund expires in June and can only be renewed via constitutional amendment, a tricky prospect given that much of Congress resents relaxing its influence over the budget.
Brasilia University politics professor David Fleischer saw other pitfalls ahead for the government.

One was a bill under study in the Senate which would restrict the president's ability to issue decrees. Another was a potentially bruising fight between government-allied parties over who gets to oversee a bill detailing privatization of Brazil's massive telecommunications industry.
"The government has a lot of things on the fire," Fleischer said. "It is going to have be attentive and smart."
